resources.string: Earth → Moon → Mars → Jupiter. Fly past our nearest neighbor, the red planet and a giant without stopping.
Earth → Moon → Venus → Mercury. Pass the Moon and swing by the real inner planets.
Earth → Moon → Venus → Mars. Pass the Moon and cloudy Venus on the way to the red planet.
Earth → Moon → Mars → Jupiter → Saturn → Uranus. A long voyage past a succession of real worlds.
Earth → Moon → Mars → Jupiter → Pluto. An imagined route adding lunar and Mars flybys to the Jupiter–Pluto encounter order.
Earth → Moon → Jupiter → Saturn → Uranus → Neptune. Pass the Moon before following the outer-planet encounter order of Voyager 2.
An imagined flyby itinerary linking real worlds. Scale, timing and trajectories serve the focus session, not a calculated navigation plan.
Earth → Moon → Jupiter → Proxima Centauri b. Leave the solar system for a detected planet around our nearest stellar neighbor.
Earth → Moon → Jupiter → TRAPPIST-1 e → f → g. Leave the solar system and pass three observed planets in one system from inner to outer orbit.
Earth → Moon → Jupiter → LHS 1140 b. Solar-system flybys precede a visit to this JWST atmospheric research target.
Earth → Moon → Jupiter → TOI-700 e → d. Leave the solar system, then pass two small planets in the same system.
Earth → Moon → Venus → 55 Cancri e. Pass nearby solar-system worlds before observing a hot super-Earth.
Radial-velocity detection. Surface and atmosphere remain unconfirmed; the view is an artist interpretation.
Transit observations confirm these planets. Surface water and habitability are not established; scenery is interpretive.
JWST studies test atmospheric and water-rich scenarios. An ocean is not confirmed; the icy view is one interpretation.
TESS transit detections. Habitable-zone location does not establish water or life; surfaces are artist interpretations.
JWST thermal spectroscopy motivates an extremely hot world with a possible secondary atmosphere. Surface detail is interpretive.
